WalkthroughText: An array is a fixed-size, ordered collection of values of the same type, stored in consecutive slots. Each slot has an index, and in Java indexing always starts at 0, so an array with n elements has valid indices 0 through n-1. You create an array either by listing values in curly braces or by using the new keyword with a size, like new int[4], which reserves 4 slots all set to a default value (0 for int). Accessing arr[i] retrieves the value at position i, but if i is negative or i is greater than or equal to the array's length, Java throws an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of silently giving you a wrong answer.

PracticeItems.Explanation: Array indices start at 0, so nums[0]=10, nums[1]=20, nums[2]=30, nums[3]=40. nums[2] is 30, not 20 (that would be nums[1]) or 40 (that would be nums[3]).

PracticeItems.Prompt: Which line of code correctly creates an array of 5 integers, all initialized to 0?
PracticeItems.Explanation: The correct syntax uses new int[5] with square brackets to specify the size, producing an array of 5 elements all defaulted to 0. new int(4) is invalid because arrays use brackets not parentheses, and int[4] would only make 4 elements, off by one from the required 5, while int[5] arr is invalid syntax for declaring an array.

The array vals has valid indices 0, 1, and 2 (length 3). Index 3 is out of bounds, which causes an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at runtime rather than printing 25 (the last valid element, at index 2) or a default value.

WalkthroughSteps.Caption: Let's declare and create an array of 4 integers using new int[4]. This reserves 4 consecutive slots, all starting at the default value 0.
Each slot in the strip has an index label starting at 0, so the valid indices here are 0, 1, 2, and 3 — never 4.
Now let's write the value 10 into index 0 using arr[0] = 10.
Next we write 20 into index 1 with arr[1] = 20.
We write 30 into index 2 with arr[2] = 30.
Finally we write 40 into index 3 with arr[3] = 40. Notice the last valid index is 3, which is one less than the length (4).
To read a value, we use the same index notation. arr[2] resolves to 30 — the value stored in slot 2 of the strip.
But what if we try arr[4]? There is no slot 4 on this strip — the highest index is 3. Accessing it throws an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
The rule to remember: for an array of length n, valid indices run from 0 to n-1. Stepping outside that range always crashes the program.
